## DOGS & GIRLS & GHOULS
## REVISED WRITING STYLE, VOICE, DIALOGUE, PACING & INTIMACY
## REFERENCE
A chapter-grounded reference to Somanoko’s Dogs & Girls & Ghouls (Oh my!) —
## Chapters 1–90
## REVISED EDITION • CHAPTER EVIDENCE INDEX • STYLE & FORMAT
## NOTES
DGG Writing Reference • Somanoko • 1How to use this reference
This revision keeps the useful structure of the earlier reference but replaces
unsupported generalisations with
chapter-specific evidence. It is a practical guide to what Somanoko actually does on
the page: how narration moves, how
dialogue is punctuated, how characters sound, how scenes breathe, and how intimacy
is written across different stages of
Aika and Uta’s relationship.
The source is the supplied 1,867-page PDF. The story text occupies approximately
PDF pages 12–1,310, followed by
additional canon and writing-reference material. The chapter index in the PDF has a
few numbering inconsistencies and an
interlude inserted after Chapter 43. This guide follows the numbered chapter titles
and the story text where they differ; it
does not silently “correct” Somanoko’s numbering.
Page references below mean pages in the supplied PDF, not AO3 page numbers. The
chapter locator is intended to make
it possible to return to the primary text. Where a chapter heading is missing,
duplicated, or displaced in the PDF export,
the locator says so rather than pretending the boundary is cleaner than it is.
This is not a claim that every sentence is a model sentence or that every punctuation
choice is deliberate. The point is to
preserve the source’s real texture—including its looseness, repetitions, abrupt shifts,
occasional awkwardness, author
notes, humour, and uneven polish—rather than editing it into a different writer’s style.
- The actual narrative voice

The dominant mode is close first-person narration through Aika. Her personality is
not confined to spoken dialogue: it
shapes what she notices, what she overlooks, how she describes people, what she
assumes, and how quickly her thoughts
move from one subject to another. The opening of Chapter 1 (PDF p. 12) moves from
customer-service cheerfulness to
private irritation, then to the danger of the Fourth Ward, then to her attachment to
Bjorn. Her narration can be funny,
blunt, self-mocking, anxious, observant, and unexpectedly serious in quick succession.
Aika’s narration often thinks while it speaks. She starts an explanation, qualifies it,
remembers something else, changes
direction, or undercuts her own point. That is not a flaw to be automatically removed.
In Chapter 43 (pp. 711–762), an
ordinary conversation in the studio about a problem with a neighbour takes its time
before the chapter moves toward
intimacy. The scene is allowed to begin as a conversation rather than announcing its
eventual destination.
The story is not locked to Aika’s first person at all times. It includes passages from
Uta’s perspective and third-person
passages that reveal what he notices or thinks. Chapter 43 contains a shift into Uta’s
thoughts after the shared scene;
Chapter 57 includes a passage centred on Uta’s guilt; later chapters also use his
viewpoint to expose the difference
between what he says and what he is thinking. Do not force every scene into Aika’s
internal voice if the source chapter
deliberately changes perspective.
The narration can be expansive, then suddenly blunt. It can dwell on a mundane
detail and then land on a disturbing
realisation without a formal transition. Aika may be dramatic about a small
inconvenience and matter-of-fact about
something frightening. That contrast is part of the voice.
- Sentence rhythm, paragraphing and pacing
Somanoko varies sentence length. Longer sentences often carry several linked
observations, qualifications, or physical
details. Short sentences isolate a reaction or let a thought land: “Gross.” in Chapter 1
is a complete paragraph. Elsewhere
a one-line thought, a repeated word, or a fragment gives the reader a beat before the
next action.
Paragraphs are not all the same size. A paragraph may contain dialogue, an action
beat, and Aika’s interpretation
together; another may be only a few words. Dialogue is often separated into its own
paragraph, but the prose does not
follow a rigid screenplay pattern. The spacing creates pauses, particularly in scenes
where Aika watches Uta work, waits

for him to answer, or struggles to say something.
Pacing follows the scene’s immediate purpose. Chapters 28–38 include work, food,
parties, domestic routines, training,
and relationship development; they are not all driven by a crisis. Chapter 30, “Movie
Night,” is a useful reference for quiet
shared time. Chapter 38 is explicitly framed by the author as domestic material. Those
chapters show that a scene can
remain ordinary and still matter.
The story also uses abrupt escalation. Chapters 5–7 move from a lurking danger
toward Aika recognising what Uta is;
Chapters 40–43 move through danger and its aftermath into an explicit
relationship/intimacy chapter. Chapters 83–87
become much harsher and slower in their consequences. Do not smooth all these
modes into one uniform pace.
DGG Writing Reference • Somanoko • 2Time skips are stated plainly when useful.
Chapter 49 announces a five-month jump (“5 Months Later (Mid June)”) and
then returns to ordinary work and planning. Chapter 44, “The Morning After,”
resumes after the long posting gap and
focuses on aftermath. A time skip should not erase the emotional and physical
consequences that remain.
- Punctuation and typography: what the PDF actually
shows
Commas: Somanoko frequently uses commas to keep a thought moving through
observation, action, and qualification.
The sentences can be conversational and cumulative rather than tightly compressed.
Do not break every long sentence
into polished, evenly balanced clauses. At the same time, do not imitate comma
density mechanically; use it when the
viewpoint is moving through several linked impressions.
Semicolons: Semicolons do appear in the story, including in early narration. Chapter
1 (PDF p. 13) has “stay later; and
alone with him,” and the same early chapter uses “Whatever it had been; he was a
giant fluffy ball...
”. These examples
show that semicolons are part of the source’s punctuation, but they are not a strict
signature that must appear in every
chapter. Some are loose or nonstandard. Preserve the voice where the meaning is
clear; do not insert semicolons just to
make prose look more literary.
Ellipses: Ellipses are a frequent part of hesitation, trailing speech, uncertainty, and
emotional restraint. Both three-dot
forms and the single Unicode ellipsis occur. Chapter 43 uses hesitant dialogue such as
“Uta...I’ve got something to tell
you...” and “Well... Ms. Kirin...

”. Chapter 86 uses ellipses to show Aika’s fractured processing after eating human
flesh.
The pauses are not interchangeable with em dashes: ellipses tend to trail, hesitate, or
leave something unsaid.
Em dashes and hyphens: The story uses dashes for interruptions, sudden changes in
thought, and cut-off dialogue, as well
as hyphens in ordinary compounds. In dialogue, a dash can show a speaker being
interrupted or changing direction before
finishing. Do not replace every dash with an ellipsis; they create different rhythms.
Exclamation marks, capitals, elongated words and informal spelling: Aika’s
excitement, embarrassment, irritation, and
teasing can be visibly loud on the page. Chapter 1 opens with “Okaaaaay!” and later
uses “Gross.” as a contrasting
deadpan beat. The source also uses repeated punctuation, stretched words,
contractions, casual spellings, and occasional
profanity. These are voice tools, not decorations to add to every line.
Italics: The PDF visibly preserves selective italics. They can emphasise a word inside
narration, distinguish an internal
thought, or change the tone of a sentence. On PDF p. 1,000, “ripping” is italicised
inside an action sentence. On PDF p.
1,195, “growled” and “stare” are italicised in narration, and “Mmmm. Steak might be
nice for dinner.” appears as an
italicised thought. The italicisation is selective; it does not mean every thought needs
italics.
Bold: Bold emphasis is also present, but it is occasional rather than a constant prose
effect. On PDF p. 1,195, “Bacon” is
bolded within Aika’s spoken line. In an author note on the same page, the literal
characters “**PAIN**” appear in the
exported text; distinguish that visible Markdown-style notation in a note from actual
bold formatting in the story body. Do
not assume that every dramatic word should be bold.
Bold italics: The supplied PDF supports selective bold and selective italics, but it does
not establish bold-italic as a
universal or frequent rule. Use combined emphasis only when a specific source
passage visibly uses it. Do not invent a
formatting system or apply bold italics to every intense thought.
Scene separators: The source uses visible breaks such as a centred dot (•) and heart
symbols (
♥), as well as blank space.
These breaks can mark a shift in viewpoint, time, or scene. Keep them when matching
a chapter’s structure instead of
replacing every break with a conventional chapter-style divider.
- Dialogue: tags, action beats and conversation
Dialogue is generally presented in quotation marks and embedded in prose it’s not
separated from paragraphs sometimes it’s at the top and sometimes at the end of the

paragraph it’s not always in between paragraphs separated. The speaker is usually
clear through a
conventional tag (“said,” “asked,” “called,” “muttered,” “whispered”) or through an
action beat that identifies who moved
or reacted. In the story text, “said” is the most common tag; “asked,” “called,”
“muttered,” “added,” and “whispered”
also recur. The reference should not encourage replacing ordinary tags with elaborate
synonyms.
A tag and an action beat do different jobs. A tag identifies the act of speaking; an
action beat gives the reader a physical
event or reaction. Chapter 43 pairs Aika’s quiet explanation with Uta’s hands pausing
over his work, his posture changing,
and his attention shifting to her. The physical response carries information that a line
such as “he said angrily” would
flatten.
DGG Writing Reference • Somanoko • 3Dialogue can be short and unadorned. Uta’s
“Hum?” in Chapter 43 is enough to keep the exchange moving. He does not
need a cryptic speech every time he answers. He can also speak in longer, casual
passages when he is explaining
something, teasing, or discussing a practical matter.
Aika’s speech often includes contractions, repetitions, self-corrections, direct questions,
exclamations, and unfinished
thoughts. She can be blunt or profane; she can also be diplomatic, careful, or soft
when the situation calls for it. Do not
turn her into a constant quip machine.
Conversation sometimes overlaps or moves quickly. In Chapter 43, Aika begins
explaining before Uta has fully reacted; in
later domestic scenes, they interrupt, answer only part of a question, or let a pause
stand. Do not force every exchange
into perfectly balanced turn-taking.
Use dialogue tags in a natural distribution. A clear “said” is better than a string of
conspicuous alternatives. Let a gesture,
a change in posture, a look, a task continuing, or silence carry the beat when the
speaker is already obvious. Avoid
attaching an action to every single line; the source also allows plain dialogue.
- Aika’s voice
Aika’s voice is immediate and personal. She can be casual, spontaneous, sarcastic,
embarrassed, anxious, affectionate,
blunt, profane, or composed. Her internal narration can ramble and double back. She
often notices practical details and
then reacts emotionally to what those details mean.
Her humour is often situational and self-aware. In Chapter 1 she is cheerful to
customers while privately imagining

violence toward rude people; the contrast is funny because it belongs to her situation,
not because she is delivering a
polished joke. She can also be silly with Bjorn, tease Uta, or make up names for
people. That humour should disappear or
quiet down when the scene is genuinely frightening.
Aika’s speech changes with safety and emotional pressure. When she feels
comfortable, she can be expansive and
teasing. When frightened, hurt, or overwhelmed, she may hesitate, repeat herself, trail
off, or say very little. Chapter 86 is
particularly important: after her first full Ghoul meal, the narration becomes
fragmented and sensory, and she struggles to
process what she has done. Do not make her equally articulate in every emotional
state.
Her narration should reflect what she knows at that point in the story. Early Aika does
not understand Ghoul society or
biology the way later Aika does. After her transformation, the sensory and physical
world changes. Her vocabulary,
assumptions, and bodily awareness should develop rather than being retroactively
identical from Chapter 1.
- Uta’s voice
Uta’s dialogue is relaxed, observant, and often understated, but he is not restricted to
cryptic one-liners. He can answer
simply, tease, explain, discuss practical matters, become blunt, or carry on a longer
conversation. The right amount of
speech depends on the person, the subject, and his emotional state.
His humour is frequently dry or casually strange. He may say something alarming in
an ordinary tone, or make a practical
observation while Aika is still processing the situation. He does not need to smirk after
every line. His expression and body
language can be much quieter than his actual thoughts.
Uta’s affection is often physical and habitual: staying close, touching, adjusting
something, watching, carrying, making
something, or noticing a change in Aika. It can be possessive or playful, but it is not
always overtly seductive. Chapter 43
shows him continuing to work while Aika watches, then stopping when he understands
that something is wrong. Chapters
81–82 show him planning and carrying out a date, including the practical details
around Aika’s needs.
When the narrative enters Uta’s viewpoint, his thoughts can be more direct,
possessive, strange, or emotionally revealing
than his spoken words. Chapter 57 is a useful reference for guilt after he has hurt Aika.
Chapter 82 also gives access to his
planning and his interpretation of her reactions. Do not make his internal voice
identical to Aika’s.

- Other character voices
Renji’s speech is direct, practical, and often protective. He can be blunt with Aika
while still treating her as family. He does
not need to sound like a formal caretaker in every scene. Chapters 86–87 are
particularly useful for his role during Aika’s
first days as a Ghoul: he gives instructions, watches her condition, and deals with the
immediate needs of feeding and
recovery.
DGG Writing Reference • Somanoko • 4Shuu’s speech and behaviour can be
theatrical, expressive, and socially performative, but he should not become a
single-note caricature. Itori, Touka, Hinami, Kazuha, Hiroshi, and others each have
distinct relationships with Aika and Uta.
Their vocabulary and level of formality should follow those relationships and the
situation.
Children and frightened characters should not automatically sound cheeky or
precocious. Yuto’s speech changes with his
sense of safety. When frightened, his starts and repetitions become more obvious;
when comfortable, he can be more
direct and playful. Use the scene-specific evidence rather than a generic “energetic
child” voice.
- Sexual intimacy and physical affection: chapter evidence
The intimate writing changes across the story. It is not one fixed “smut style,” and not
every intimate moment is sexual. But it is explicit and unfiltered.
The chapters below are the strongest reference points for different kinds of intimacy;
consult the whole scene in the
source rather than copying a single gesture.
Chapter 43 (PDF pp. 711–762; first explicit-content chapter): The chapter begins with
an ordinary return to the studio, a
conversation, and a quiet shared space. The intimacy grows out of that scene rather
than starting with a sudden seduction
cue. Somanoko’s author note openly says this was new territory for her and that she
was nervous about writing it. This
chapter is useful for the transition from conversation to sexual intimacy and for seeing
the early version of their physical
relationship.
Chapter 49, “Time Flies” (PDF pp. 840–854): The chapter uses a five-month time skip
and includes a small “lemon”
section. It is useful for comparing intimacy after the relationship has had more time to
settle. The scene is a smaller insert
rather than a full chapter built entirely around sex.
Chapter 54 (PDF pp. 894–904): The author labels the chapter “mostly” lemon and
comments on Uta’s blood kink. It is a
strong reference for the overlap between Ghoul biology, blood, biting, appetite, and
sexual intimacy. Do not separate the

physical danger and the affection into unrelated categories; in this relationship they
can coexist, but the scene’s context
and consent still matter.
Chapter 62, “(Almost) Time to Go” (PDF pp. 992–1005): This is a pre-auction
chapter in which Uta is unusually close and
attentive. It is useful for reading how anticipation, practical preparation, and physical
familiarity coexist. The intimacy is
embedded in a day with a clear external event approaching.
Chapter 81, “All Hallows Eve” (PDF pp. 1,237–1,244): The opening gives Uta’s
viewpoint as he prepares to leave. His
reading of Aika’s “Be safe” rather than “Have fun” is an example of intimacy
conveyed through his interpretation of a
small exchange. The chapter is useful for the relationship continuing in ordinary
domestic space even while Uta leaves for
Ghoul business.
Chapter 82, “Date Night” (PDF pp. 1,245–1,251): This chapter is explicitly framed as
fluff/date night, but it also includes
adult intimacy and Uta’s perspective. It is useful for how affection, humour, date
logistics, the lack of ordinary human
food, and sexual familiarity sit in the same chapter. Do not reduce it to either “cute
date” or “sex scene”; it contains both.
Chapter 89, “Marked” (PDF pp. 1,298–1,305): This is important for the changed
physical and emotional context after
Aika’s transformation. Marking and biting are now tied to her own Ghoul instincts as
well as their established relationship.
Do not write this as though Aika’s new body simply erases her previous human
feelings.
Chapter 90, “Gaslight. Gatekeep. Girlboss” (PDF pp. 1,306 onward): The author note
says the mood was interrupted and
that recovery does not happen in a day. This is a useful corrective against assuming
every opportunity for intimacy must
become sex. Physical recovery, awkwardness, care, and ordinary teasing can interrupt
the expected mood.
Across these chapters, intimacy can be tender, playful, hungry, awkward, possessive,
funny, physically intense, or
interrupted. Biting and marks may be affectionate, sexual, or Ghoul-specific; they are
not automatically interchangeable.
Track who initiates, what each character wants, what the body can do, whether
anyone is injured or recovering, and what
the characters understand about the consequences.
- Ghoul biology and physical continuity inside intimate
scenes
The story’s Ghoul physiology is not decorative. Ghouls eat human flesh; ordinary
human food is foul and not properly

digestible; plain coffee is an exception. Scent, blood, appetite, regeneration, kagune,
RC-cell changes, and physical
durability affect what characters can do and how they experience touch.
DGG Writing Reference • Somanoko • 5Aika’s transformation changes her sensory
and physical experience gradually. Chapter 86, “Day 1 Ghoul,” is essential for
the immediate bodily and emotional consequences of eating human flesh. Chapter 87
continues the adjustment and the
practical care around it. Chapter 89 shows the emerging instincts and changed
intimacy. Do not give Aika full control or
perfect understanding immediately after transformation.
A Ghoul’s skin is extremely tough; ordinary weapons do not pierce it, while Quinque
can. Injuries, regeneration, and
physical limitations should remain consistent with the story’s established rules. A
kagune is a biological organ, not a
magical prop. Its movement and contact should follow the character’s body and the
scene’s physical geography.
Sexual and affectionate scenes must still respect physical continuity: where hands are,
what is being held, who moves
first, how a character responds, what clothing or furniture is in the way, and whether
an injury or recovery period limits
movement. Do not let bodies teleport between positions simply to reach the next beat.
- Chapter-by-chapter evidence locator
The list below is a navigation index, not a plot summary. It records the chapter
label/title and the PDF page where the
chapter begins or where its opening is located. Use the chapter itself for the full
evidence. An interlude follows Chapter 43
and is listed separately.
- Practical drafting checklist
Before drafting, establish: (1) the chapter and date in the story timeline; (2) the
viewpoint character; (3) what that
character knows at this point; (4) what they are physically doing; (5) the emotional
temperature of the scene; and (6)
whether the scene is domestic, comic, frightening, violent, sexual, or some mixture.
Then let the prose follow the scene. Use commas when the thought moves through
linked observations; semicolons only
when they arise naturally; ellipses for trailing or hesitation; dashes for interruption;
italics or bold only where emphasis is
warranted. Do not make every line witty, every pause meaningful, every touch
seductive, or every paragraph elegant.
For dialogue, use ordinary tags where they are clear. Let action beats and silence do
some of the work. Keep Aika’s
speech immediate and changeable. Keep Uta’s speech varied, relaxed, and observant
without reducing him to cryptic
teasing. Let the other characters retain their own rhythms.

For intimacy, identify the specific chapter reference that best matches the moment:
Chapter 43 for early explicit intimacy,
49 for a small later insert, 54 for blood/Ghoul intimacy, 62 for pre-auction closeness,
81–82 for established domestic/date
intimacy, 89 for post-transformation marking, and 90 for recovery interrupting sex.
Do not copy a scene without checking
the characters’ current physical and emotional circumstances.
The final edit should correct confusion and continuity errors, not erase the source’s
informal texture. Preserve
awkwardness when it belongs to the character; preserve repetition when it conveys
emotion; preserve ordinary
conversation when nothing dramatic needs to happen.

PDF page numbers refer to the supplied PDF. The interlude is listed separately
because it appears after Chapter 43 and is
not one of the numbered chapters in this 1–90 locator.

Short source examples to keep in view
- Chapter 1, PDF p. 12: “Gross.” — a one-word paragraph that cuts against the
preceding longer narration.
DGG Writing Reference • Somanoko • 9• Chapter 1, PDF p. 13: “stay later; and
alone with him” — a real semicolon example, including the source’s loose usage.
- Chapter 43, PDF pp. 711–762: “Uta...I’ve got something to tell you...” — hesitation
and trailing speech before a difficult
conversation.
- Chapter 77, PDF p. 1,195: “Mmmm. Steak might be nice for dinner.” — italicised
internal thought; the same page uses
selective bold and italics elsewhere.
- Chapter 86, PDF pp. 1,268 onward: “I’d eaten... someone.” — ellipsis and spacing
help represent Aika’s shock and delayed
processing.
DGG Writing Reference • Somanoko • 10Detailed evidence addendum
Concrete chapter examples for dialogue tags, punctuation, typography, and intimacy.
Page numbers refer to the
supplied source PDF.
A. Dialogue tags and action beats — actual examples
- Chapter 1, PDF p. 13: “Have a goodnight!!!” I called out cheerfully — a
conventional tag identifies the speaker, while
“cheerfully” gives the delivery. The exaggerated punctuation belongs to the public-
facing Aika in this moment.
- Chapter 43, PDF p. 711: “Thank you for coming to get me.” I said softly, seating
myself... — a simple “said” tag is paired
with an action beat and a delivery word. The physical action is not replaced by an
elaborate speech verb.
- Chapter 43, PDF p. 712: “Did she bother you again?” — Uta’s question follows a
physical change: his hands stop, he sits
straighter, and his attention leaves his work. The action before the line does the
emotional work.
- Chapter 86, PDF p. 1,269: “...Full, finally?” Renji questioned. He flipped the seared
meat over... — the question tag is
followed by continued action, keeping the exchange grounded in what Renji is doing.
- Chapter 86, PDF p. 1,270: “Sure Ai-chan. I’ll make sure not to go far.” His face was
blank but his eyes glimmered
mischievously. — the next sentence is an action/description beat, not another
dialogue tag. The contrast between face
and eyes supplies the tone.
B. Punctuation patterns — do not flatten the differences

- Comma-led thought: Chapter 1 repeatedly lets Aika’s observation expand through
linked clauses and qualifications.
Preserve that conversational movement when it is clear; do not split every long
sentence into short, polished
statements.
- Semicolon: Chapter 1, PDF p. 13: “stay later; and alone with him.” Chapter 1 also
has “Whatever it had been; he was a
giant fluffy ball...
”. These are genuine examples, but the usage is loose. They prove the mark occurs;
they do not
establish a rule to use it frequently.
- Ellipsis: Chapter 43, PDF p. 712: “Uta...I’ve got something to tell you...” The pause
signals hesitation and an unfinished
emotional approach. Chapter 86 uses the single-character ellipsis in Aika’s shocked
processing: “I’d eaten... someone.”
- Em dash: In later chapters, dashes often mark a cut-off, interruption, or sharp turn in
thought. Keep the distinction: an
ellipsis trails or hesitates; a dash breaks or interrupts.
- Italics: Chapter 77, PDF p. 1,195: “Mmmm. Steak might be nice for dinner.” is set
as an italicised thought. The same page
italicises selected words in narration, including “growled” and “stare.” Chapter 43 and
Chapter 86 also use pauses and
emphasis without needing every thought italicised.
- Bold: Chapter 77, PDF p. 1,195 bolds “Bacon” within dialogue. Bold is selective and
can mark a particular word for vocal
stress. Do not bold every loud or emotional word.
- Combined bold and italics: The supplied PDF shows selective bold and italics, but
does not establish combined bold-italic
as a frequent house style. Match a combined treatment only when the specific source
passage visibly uses it.
C. Intimacy scenes — what each chapter is actually useful for
- Chapter 43: The scene does not open as a sex scene. Aika returns to the studio; Uta
is working; she thanks him; quiet
and a difficult conversation come first. The scene’s movement from ordinary talk to
intimacy is the useful craft lesson.
The author note says this was new territory for Somanoko and that she felt nervous
about writing it.
- Chapter 49: The chapter explicitly marks a five-month time jump and labels the
intimate material as a small “lemon”
insert. It is a later-stage relationship reference, not a template for a whole chapter
devoted to sex.
- Chapter 54: The author note calls the chapter mostly lemon and comments on Uta’s
blood kink. It is a strong source for

the overlap between blood, biting, appetite, and sexual intimacy. The Ghoul element
is part of the physical scene, not a
decorative detail.
- Chapter 62: Uta is unusually touch-oriented in the lead-up to the Auction. The
intimacy is framed by anticipation,
preparation, and the fact that he has a plan. Use it when a scene needs closeness
alongside an external event.
- Chapter 81: The opening is in Uta’s viewpoint. He reads the difference between
Aika saying “Be safe” and “Have fun,”
then responds to her concern. This is an example of intimacy conveyed by
interpretation and small domestic exchanges
rather than explicit description.
DGG Writing Reference • Evidence Addendum • 1• Chapter 82: The chapter is
explicitly framed as a date-night/fluff chapter, but it also contains adult intimacy. It
moves
between the date, practical Ghoul limitations, humour, and the couple’s established
physical familiarity. Keep those
registers together.
- Chapter 89: After Aika’s transformation, marking and biting take on a changed
bodily context. Aika is not merely the
recipient of Uta’s Ghoul behaviour; her own instincts and desire to mark him matter.
- Chapter 90: The author note says the mood was interrupted and recovery takes
time. This is a crucial counterexample to
the assumption that every intimate opportunity must become sex. Injury, recovery,
emotional readiness, and ordinary
care can change the scene.
D. What not to infer from the evidence
- Do not turn examples into rules: A semicolon in Chapter 1 does not mean every
paragraph needs one. An italicised
thought in Chapter 77 does not mean all thoughts should be italicised. A bold word
does not mean shouting should be
bold.
- Do not over-romanticise: The source includes ordinary, practical, awkward, silly,
and sometimes uncomfortable
conversation. Aika and Uta do not need to make every exchange meaningful or
seductive.
- Do not over-sanitise: The source can be blunt, repetitive, messy, horny, violent,
sentimental, or funny. Correct only what
makes the meaning or continuity unclear.
- Do not erase the body: In intimate and recovery scenes, track injury, regeneration,
appetite, scent, skin, kagune, and also If writing a past chapter do not erase human
vulnerability to Uta, Uta still can bite hard and leave marks and also Ghouls still react
to blood and cuts and scent so yeah. And also as well Utas still eats eyeballs don’t
forget that.

clothing, and physical position. Ghoul biology changes the scene’s possibilities.
Chapter paragraphs and words fill whole page so no small lines.

## DOGS & GIRLS & GHOULS (OH MY!)
## Information & Continuity Reference — Chapters 1–90
Somanoko • Source-grounded working reference
Prepared as a separate information reference for Somanoko’s DGG. This document
records story events, relationship development, important conversations, continuity,
and source-grounded interpretation. It is not a replacement for the original chapters or
the separate writing-style reference.
Navigation: relationship arc • important dialogue • intimacy continuity • weapons and
Ghoul biology • chapter locator • corrections/research limits
Scope, source handling, and timeline cautions
Source and attribution
This reference concerns Somanoko’s story, Dogs & Girls & Ghouls (Oh my!), Chapters
1–90. The story and its characters belong to Somanoko; this document is a research
aid, not a claim of authorship.
The source PDF includes the story text and additional reference material appended
after the chapters. Where possible, chapter-scene details below are distinguished
from later working-reference summaries. The original chapter text remains the
authority if a summary conflicts with it.
Publication/index dates shown in the PDF’s chapter index are not automatically story-
calendar dates. Somanoko’s posting gaps do not mean an equivalent amount of story
time passed. Do not infer story chronology from publication dates.
Timeline facts to preserve
The first meeting is October 31, 2020. Aika returns to Uta’s shop two days later; the
user’s established date for that return is November 3, 2020. The calendar arithmetic
between October 31 and November 3 is not silently reconciled here; retain the user-
specified story date pending a direct chapter-level check.
The first Anteiku visit is Saturday, November 7, 2020. Uta invites Aika; the reason and
surrounding context are in the early chapters. After that visit, Aika does not return for
the next seven days because Uta asks her not to come while he works on her mask.
December 6, 2020 is the rooftop outing in Chapter 17. It is not a date. December 24 is
their first official date. December 31 is when they officially become a couple. On
January 1, after the New Year festival, Uta asks Aika to stay/move in and gives her a key.
The five-month jump around Chapter 49 is a story-time jump to mid-June. The 2023
dates in the index are posting dates, not evidence that the story has jumped to 2023.

At the end of Chapter 90, the story calendar is December 9, 2021? The source
reference material gives a December 9, 2023 label while also stating that Aika and Uta
have known each other about one year and three months and that she has been a
Ghoul for about a week. These statements are internally inconsistent with the
established October 31, 2020 first meeting. Treat the exact end-date/year as
unresolved until the original Chapter 90 date line is reconciled; do not use posting
dates as a shortcut.
How to read this reference
Direct quotations are kept short and are reproduced only where the wording is
important. Longer passages are summarized rather than copied.
Interpretation is labelled as interpretation. A character’s fear, intention, or emotional
subtext should not be presented as an explicit fact unless the narration or dialogue
establishes it.
Chapter numbering in the PDF’s index contains an apparent numbering irregularity
around Chapters 61–63 and interludes. Use the chapter title as well as the number
when locating those sections.
Relationship arc: Aika and Uta
- First meeting and the repeated visits — Chapters 1–4
Aika first meets Uta at HySy ArtMask Studio on October 31, 2020, when she
commissions a mask made from animal skulls. Their early interactions are not yet a
romance. Aika is curious, socially self-conscious at moments, and increasingly
comfortable returning to the shop; Uta is observant, polite, and interested in her as a
customer and person.
Aika returns with the skulls and Uta works with them. He gets her number and invites
her to Anteiku. The coffee and donuts become part of their early shared routine. Uta’s
invitation is significant because it moves their contact beyond a strictly commercial
mask commission.
Uta later explains that he initially expected Aika might leave his shop and never return.
Her continued visits surprised him. Do not rewrite the early visits as a conscious
courtship by either character; the importance is that a casual pattern becomes
personally meaningful to Uta.
- Anteiku, the mask, and the first signs of danger — Chapters 3–8
Aika’s first Anteiku visit is November 7, 2020, with Uta. She meets people who will
become part of her social world. Uta asks her not to visit for a week while he finishes
her mask as a surprise; Aika misreads the request as possible rejection or annoyance.
Mr. Fuji breaks into Aika’s apartment and attacks Bjorn. Aika fights back with rebar and
takes Bjorn to Uta’s home. Uta helps her, makes coffee, and takes practical steps to
help secure the apartment. This is one of the first occasions when his care is shown
through action rather than a declaration.

In Chapter 6, while Aika is staying at Uta’s, she asks what Ghouls are like as people:
what they enjoy, their hobbies, interests, and favourite colours. Uta explains that they
can be like anyone else she has met; they blend in and survive. The exchange
establishes Aika’s attempt to understand Ghouls as people before she fully
understands Uta’s identity.
In Chapter 7, Aika asks permission and removes Uta’s glasses, seeing his kakugan. She
has been ignoring signs but now faces the truth. Uta tells her he will not eat her and
explains Bjorn’s ability to detect Ghouls. His warning about Tsukiyama foreshadows
the danger in Aika’s social circle.
- Tsukiyama, Itori, and Aika’s place in the Ghoul world — Chapters 8–16
Aika reunites with childhood friend Shuu Tsukiyama in Chapters 9–10. This
reintroduces a relationship from her human life into the increasingly complicated
Ghoul world. Her familiarity with Shuu does not mean she understands his current
activities or the danger around him.
Aika meets Nico and spends time at Helter Skelter on December 5, 2020. The bar
becomes an important place for conversations about Ghoul culture and the history
shared by Uta, Renji, and Itori. Itori’s stories are sometimes exaggerated; Uta and Renji
interject to correct or qualify them.
Chapter 15 includes Aika confronting Uta about the dead mugger. Uta explains that he
followed her to keep her safe and that the man was already dead when Aika told him
about the attack. The conversation forces Aika to confront that Uta’s protection can
involve lethal violence. It is important not to flatten this into uncomplicated approval or
uncomplicated condemnation: Aika wants honesty, is disturbed, and continues
negotiating what she can accept.
Chapters 14–16 build toward the rooftop surprise. The relationship is becoming more
familiar, but Aika remains human and vulnerable in a world where Uta’s physical
capabilities and Ghoul instincts are very different from hers.
- The rooftop and the “kept coming back” conversation — Chapter 17
On December 6, 2020, Uta takes Aika up the side of a skyscraper with her eyes closed.
The outing is explicitly not a date. He explains that he did not want to scare her away
and had initially thought she might leave his shop and never visit again.
Key short quotation: “...but you kept coming back. You always came back.”
The context is essential: Uta is talking about the pattern of her returning to his shop,
not claiming that Aika had already promised him a relationship. Her visits were her
choice; he noticed them and came to value them. His earlier fear of frightening her
away becomes explicit.
When Aika panics during the climb, Uta tells her to ease her grip and promises that she
will not fall because he has her. At the top, she sits in front of him, between his legs,
with his arms around her waist. The physical arrangement is practical as well as
intimate: he is keeping her secure while sharing the view.

Uta also learns her scent by breathing near the crook of her neck. The scene introduces
scent as a Ghoul-specific form of recognition and closeness. CCG investigators
interrupt their return, and Aika sees a Quinque in action for the first time.
- Friendship, fear, and the meaning of “his” — Chapter 19
Aika is troubled by the way Tsukiyama treated her and by Nico’s use of words such as
“pet.” She asks what being Uta’s friend actually means. She worries that she may have
misunderstood their relationship and that a human friend might still be regarded as
food by a Ghoul.
Uta admits that she still smells delicious to him and that he has wondered what she
would taste like. He immediately places that admission beside his attachment: “But I’d
miss you if I did that. Or if I let someone else take you away...”
He explains that, in another situation, he would have killed her as soon as she
discovered what he was. Instead, he enjoyed her visits and kept letting her leave, even
after he suspected she might know. He recalls telling her on the rooftop that he wanted
her to stay close.
The narration makes the emotional contrast clear: Aika was worried whether Uta
considered her a friend; Uta was worried she would leave him. This is one of the
strongest interpretive anchors for the relationship’s early stage.
Aika challenges the language of ownership. She is not a pet, toy, or possession. Uta’s
explanation concerns Ghoul social signalling and protection: being identified as “his”
can warn other Ghouls away. Preserve the disagreement. His protective intention does
not make Aika’s objection disappear, and her objection does not mean she rejects his
care.
- Learning about each other and the wider conflict — Chapters 18–30
Chapter 18’s tattoo conversation and Chapter 20’s ink/tattoo material develop the way
Uta’s art and Aika’s willingness to let him work on her intersect. Tattoos are not merely
decoration; the scenes show negotiation, permission, artistic attention, and the
growing ease of physical proximity.
Chapter 21, “Shattered Glass,” marks a major disruption around Anteiku and the
escalating danger surrounding the Ghoul community. Chapters 22–24 move into
planning and shopping, including Aika and Itori spending time together. Their friendship
becomes more independent of Uta.
Chapter 25, “Kagune,” is the first time Aika sees Uta’s Kagune. She asks questions
about Ghoul biology and how the organ can emerge from the body. Uta explains RC
cells, the kakuhou, and Kagune as liquid muscle. He is willing to explain his biology
rather than treating her curiosity as offensive.
Chapters 26–27 involve rescue and the underground world. Chapters 28–30 move
through cooking, a party, and movie night. These chapters matter because the
relationship is not only built through danger or declarations; they also spend time
together in ordinary and social settings.
- Dating, first kisses, and choosing a shared home — Chapters 31–42

December 24 is their first official date. The date is an explicit change in how they
understand their time together, rather than simply retroactively labelling the rooftop
outing a date.
Chapter 32, “Cooking for a Ghoul,” includes Aika cooking human flesh for Uta while
she is still human. This is an important early example of her willingness to engage with
the practical realities of his diet, while preserving the fact that ordinary human food is
not suitable for Ghouls.
Chapter 34 includes Aika’s first cheek kiss with Uta while his eyes are covered,
followed by her initiating their first kiss on the lips in bed. Uta’s hesitation is tied to
having eaten recently and concern about kissing her after eating; it should not be
interpreted as a lack of desire for her.
December 31 is when they officially become a couple. Chapter 35, “New Years,” and
Chapter 36, “New Years Shine,” carry the transition into the new year. On January 1,
after the New Year festival, Uta asks Aika to stay and gives her a key. She agrees,
though her existing rental arrangements mean the move is not necessarily
instantaneous.
Chapter 37, “Blood and Tattoos,” and Chapter 38, “Ghouls can’t cook,” continue the
development of shared routines, tattoo work, care, and the ordinary compromises
required when a human and a Ghoul share a home.
- Established partnership, adult intimacy, and independent lives — Chapters 39–52
Chapters 39–42 move through old dangers, helplessness, and Uta’s return home. The
relationship is now established, but danger and emotional strain still affect how they
communicate and behave.
Chapter 43 is the first explicit sexual encounter. Chapter 44, “The Morning After,”
follows it. The morning-after material should be treated as part of their relationship
history, not as an isolated adult scene. The source includes physical familiarity,
reactions, and ordinary practical concerns.
Chapter 45, “Raw Meat,” and Chapter 46, “Girls Night Out / The Trouble with Being
Human,” broaden the story beyond the couple. Aika has her own friendships and
responsibilities; the relationship does not consume every aspect of her life.
Chapters 47–48 deal with aftermath and inheritance. Chapter 49, “Time Flies,”
contains the five-month story-time jump to mid-June. The 2023 publication date is not
the in-story date.
Chapter 50, “Semi-Hostile Takeover,” shows Aika’s business and public
responsibilities alongside domestic life. She wakes beside Uta after sex and they move
through an ordinary morning before she attends to Kogane no Shiro, Kazu, contracts,
and company matters.
Chapters 51–52, “Weekend Away” and “Family Secrets / Secret Families,” deepen the
family-history and personal-history threads that lead into Hiroshi’s role.
- Hiroshi, the Quinque, and the umbrella — Chapters 52–60

Chapter 52 reveals family secrets. Hiroshi explains that he is Aika’s paternal uncle and
that a Ghoul woman existed on her father’s side of the family. His transformation and
the family’s attempts to manage his RC levels help explain the concealed history
around Aika’s biology.
Chapter 53, “A Parting Gift (To Keep You Safe),” establishes the connection between
Hiroshi and the old CCG Quinque. It is a Bikaku-type red wakizashi/short sword, with
black leather ito, metal fuchi, and crystalline Kagune-derived structures near the hilt.
Its RC material can extend roughly four metres, curl, change direction, and follow the
sword’s movement.
Chapter 54 contains an adult intimacy scene. Chapter 55 and Chapter 56 develop the
aftermath and the weapon-concealment idea. In Chapter 56, Aika comes up with the
idea of concealing the sword inside an ordinary umbrella. Uta modifies/builds the
sheath around her idea, adding an internal sheath, a locking mechanism, and a button
release. The sword clicks securely into place; pressing the trigger releases it.
The umbrella is white with crimson spider lilies and a dark-red underside. Closed, it
looks like an ordinary umbrella. Do not say Uta independently invented the concept:
Aika proposed the concealment, and Uta engineered the mechanism.
Crystal Lily is the name Aika later gives the Quinque. It remains Hiroshi’s old CCG
Quinque, not a weapon Uta made from scratch. The small Quinque knife Uta gave Aika
is a separate object with a separate history.
Chapter 57, “Need Some Space,” is an important relationship rupture/repair point.
Aika needs room to process what has happened and to regain control over her training
and decisions. Uta’s later practical gestures, including buying donuts and respecting
her request to go out alone, function as attempts to repair rather than as a polished
verbal apology.
Chapters 58–60 develop the side effects, the reason to fight, and Aika’s name/identity
as “Wendigo.” Her CCG masked identity and her Ghoul-world identity must not be
confused.
- Auction, Yuto, and conflict — Chapters 61–78
The Auction arc changes the stakes around Aika’s role in the Ghoul world. Chapters
61–63 include the build-up and the Auction itself; the PDF index has a numbering
irregularity in this region, so use titles and scene content when citing.
Chapters 64–70 cover the aftermath, Aika’s decision to save Yuto, her conflict with Uta,
and the medical investigation into her RC levels. “Human-Tofu” becomes an important
research and household thread: a synthesized human-derived food intended to
address Ghoul nutritional needs without relying on ordinary human food.
Their disagreement about Yuto is not a simple argument over whether they like a child.
Aika is responding to a vulnerable child and her own moral commitments; Uta is
responding to danger, the practical realities of Ghoul life, and the consequences of
taking responsibility. Both are affected by the Auction and its violence.
Chapter 67, “Cold Shoulder,” and Chapter 68, “(Fighting) Like Lovers Do,” are
important for how conflict and physical familiarity coexist. Do not assume that a fight is

automatically resolved by sex or that physical closeness means the disagreement has
disappeared.
Chapters 71–72, “Vacation” and “Pool Party,” provide a deliberate pause. Aika wants
time to relax with Uta. They look at the possibility of sharing more of the household,
and she begins imagining a room where his mask-making work and her business work
can coexist. Their physical intimacy includes massage, touch, and quiet
companionship, not only sex.
Chapters 73–78 continue the consequences of the Auction, Yuto’s place in their lives,
Aika’s work, and the question of how much danger they can reasonably accept.
Chapter 74, “I bet on losing dogs,” is where Bjorn’s death occurs; the loss continues to
shape Aika’s later decisions and grief.
- Yuto, the household, and the final crisis — Chapters 79–90
Chapters 79–80 give Yuto a more sustained place in Aika’s life and show Aika trying to
build a life while still coping with grief and the physical cost of remaining human. She
continues taking RC suppressants and hides some symptoms from Uta, paralleling
earlier moments when Uta concealed his own difficulties to protect her from worry.
Chapter 81, “All Hallows Eve,” includes Uta’s perspective at the Auction. Roma
provokes him about Yuto and Aika. Uta’s response shows that he has become
protective of Yuto in his own right, not merely because Yuto matters to Aika. Uta refers
to Aika as his mate during this confrontation. This is Ghoul relationship language, not
permission to erase Aika’s autonomy.
Chapter 82, “Date Night,” is an important established-couple chapter and includes
adult intimacy. It should not be conflated with the later Chapter 89 reassurance scene.
Chapter 82 also gives access to Uta’s perspective and private thoughts, including
concern about whether he went too far and his desire to arrange another date.
Chapter 83, “Old Foes,” reveals that the CCG investigator responsible for Bjorn’s death
has tracked Aika and Uta through Bjorn’s old records. The investigator uses RC-cell
repressants and a sedative, disabling Uta’s Kagune and weakening him. Aika refuses to
abandon him. They are captured and taken to a private research/containment facility.
Chapters 84–85 cover escape and the immediate crisis. Chapter 86, “Day 1 Ghoul,”
begins Aika’s transformation. Her new biology does not erase her memories or
attachments, but it changes her sensory experience, hunger, physical capabilities, and
fear of harming Uta.
Chapter 87 continues the immediate aftermath. Uta’s recovery is gradual; his
regeneration, kakuhou, and strength do not return instantly. Aika’s separation anxiety
is pronounced: she sleeps near him and reaches toward him while asleep to check that
he is still there. When she wakes and cannot find him, she panics. Uta steps toward her
and allows her to touch him, reassuring her through action.
Chapters 88–90 continue the adjustment to Ghoul life, the changed physical
relationship, marking, and recovery. Chapter 89 contains the “Don’t leave me”
exchange. Aika’s fear is partly about the gap between them since her transformation
and her worry that she might hurt him if she cannot control herself.

Uta answers: “I will never leave you, Aika.” He tells her she is his; she answers that he
is hers too. She is also troubled that he remains unmarked. This is a mutual
commitment scene shaped by their new Ghoul circumstances, not a reversal of Aika’s
earlier rejection of being treated as property.
Chapter 90 closes the immediate recovery sequence. The final state should be read as
a couple adjusting to a recent transformation and trauma, not as a finished or
effortless resolution of every consequence.
Important dialogue and recurring emotional threads
A. “You kept coming back” — Chapters 17 and 19
Chapter 17: “...but you kept coming back. You always came back.”
Chapter 19: Uta says he enjoyed her visits and kept letting her leave even after he
thought she might suspect. He admits he wanted her to stay close but feared he might
scare her away.
Continuity meaning: Uta’s attachment develops through her repeated voluntary
returns. He does not assume her loyalty; he notices it, values it, and worries about
losing it.
B. “I’d miss you” — Chapters 19 and 62
Chapter 19: “But I’d miss you if I did that. Or if I let someone else take you away...”
Chapter 62: Uta asks whether Aika would hate him if he ate her. She answers honestly
about not wanting to die, then asks him to take care of himself if she were ever gone.
Continuity meaning: the two scenes are related but not interchangeable. Chapter 19 is
about the danger of their friendship and his attachment; Chapter 62 is a later
conversation about mortality, hunger, love, and the life they share.
C. “Stay close” — Chapters 17, 19, and later danger scenes
Chapter 17: Uta reassures Aika during the climb that he has her and promises she will
not fall.
Chapter 19: he recalls telling her he wanted her to stay close.
Later scenes use “stay close” in more practical danger contexts, including public
Ghoul spaces and the Auction. Keep the local scene context; do not turn every
instance into a romantic declaration.
D. “Don’t leave me” / “I will never leave you” — Chapter 89
Aika: “Uta. Please. Don’t leave me.”
Uta: “I will never leave you, Aika.”
Aika: “And you’re mine...”
Continuity meaning: this is a later reassurance after trauma and transformation. Aika’s
mutual claim is deliberate; her fear concerns the distance created by her new
condition and her worry about losing their established closeness.
E. Friendship is not ownership — Chapter 19 and later mate language

Aika’s objection to being called Uta’s is a genuine boundary. Uta’s explanation of
protective Ghoul signalling is part of the scene, but it does not make her a possession.
Later, Uta’s use of “mate” and mutual possessive language occurs in a relationship
that has developed and in a Ghoul social context. Preserve Aika’s agency and the fact
that the two characters can use possessive language affectionately without making
ownership their governing relationship principle.
F. Ordinary life as evidence of attachment
Chapter 62 explicitly connects love to daily routines: sleeping wrapped around each
other, coffee, talking while Uta works, and lazy evenings.
Chapter 50 demonstrates that sex, morning routines, business responsibilities, and
ordinary conversation can sit in the same sequence.
Chapter 71 shows that massages, scent, quiet time, and simply relaxing together can
be intimacy without sex.
Chapter 87 shows practical reassurance after trauma: Uta approaches rather than
withdrawing, lets Aika touch him, and does not tease her for needing proximity.
Sex, affection, and physical intimacy: continuity map
Early physical familiarity
Chapter 17: Aika sits between Uta’s legs on the rooftop; his arms secure her around
the waist. Scent recognition is introduced.
Chapters 18–20: tattoo/ink scenes involve permission, trust, and the artist/client
relationship becoming more personally familiar.
Chapter 25: Aika sees Uta’s Kagune and asks about his body and biology. Curiosity and
closeness are linked, but the conversation is not itself a sexual scene.
Dating and first sexual milestones
Chapter 31: first official date on December 24.
Chapter 34: first cheek kiss with Uta’s eyes covered; later Aika initiates their first kiss
on the lips. Preserve Uta’s concern about having eaten recently.
Chapter 35: official relationship on December 31.
Chapter 36: January 1 key and invitation to stay/move in.
Chapter 43: first explicit sexual encounter; Chapter 44 is the morning after.
Established intimacy
Chapter 49 includes a time jump and a brief adult-intimacy element. Do not misread
the publication date as the in-story date.
Chapter 50 shows morning-after comfort and the coexistence of sex and Aika’s
business responsibilities.
Chapter 54 is a significant adult intimacy scene. The scene includes Ghoul-specific
physicality and blood-related elements; retain the scene’s actual context rather than

making all later intimacy follow the same pattern. Also where Aika gave Uta head for
the first time in all the time they’ve been together.
Chapter 62 includes close physical familiarity and a conversation about the possibility
of Uta eating Aika. It is not simply a sex scene; the conversation’s emotional and
biological stakes matter.
Chapter 82 is an adult intimacy chapter from an established relationship and includes
Uta’s internal perspective. His thoughts contain desire, concern, guilt, amusement,
and practical intentions at once.
Chapter 89 includes post-transformation marking and Aika’s desire for mutual physical
recognition. Hunger and chosen intimacy must remain distinct.
Do not flatten their intimacy
Not every kiss is a short, delicate gesture. They can make out, interrupt one another,
pull each other closer, bite, laugh, and become distracted.
Not every physical interaction is sexual. Sitting together, touching hair or face,
massage, sleeping together, scenting, holding, and helping with injuries can be
ordinary affection.
Sex does not automatically resolve arguments or emotional uncertainty. Aika can enjoy
intimacy and still be upset; Uta can enjoy an encounter and still worry that he went too
far.
Keep consent and response visible. Their established familiarity does not mean
automatic agreement. Either can hesitate, refuse, change their mind, or ask for
something directly.
Preserve physical continuity: positions, clothing, movement, injuries, and reactions
should follow logically through the scene.
Weapons, identity, and Ghoul continuity
Aika’s weapons
Crystal Lily is Hiroshi’s old CCG Quinque: a Bikaku-type red wakizashi/short sword
with black leather ito, metal fuchi, and crystalline Kagune-derived structures near the
hilt. The RC material extends roughly four metres and can curl, change direction, and
follow the sword’s movement.
Aika proposes concealing the sword in an umbrella in Chapter 56. Uta builds/modifies
the umbrella sheath, including the internal sheath, lock, and button release. The
closed umbrella looks ordinary; it is white with crimson spider lilies and a dark-red
underside.
The small Quinque-steel knife Uta gave Aika is separate from Crystal Lily. Do not merge
their origins, functions, or chronology.
Aika’s CCG masked identity is Wendigo. Do not treat Wendigo as her everyday name or
as a Ghoul species.
Ghoul biology and sensory rules

Ghouls eat human flesh or appropriate human-derived material. Ordinary human food
tastes foul/like clay and is not properly digestible; it is regurgitated. Plain coffee is
acceptable and is a shared social ritual.
Ghouls have heightened senses, tough skin, enhanced physical abilities, kakugan,
kakuhou, Kagune, and regeneration. Ordinary weapons generally cannot pierce Ghoul
skin; Quinque can.
Kagune are biological organs formed from RC-cell material released through the skin
from the kakuhou. The four types are Ukaku, Koukaku, Rinkaku, and Bikaku. Individual
Kagune vary.
Human and Ghoul social realities affect food, scent, safety, territory, relationships,
and public identity. Do not make every Ghoul harmless or every Ghoul monstrous;
individual choices and values matter.
Aika’s transformation in Chapters 86–90 changes her biology and sensory experience.
It does not erase her human memories, habits, attachments, moral boundaries, or
history with Uta.
Family and supporting relationships
Hiroshi is Aika’s paternal uncle and a former CCG investigator who became a Ghoul
more than twenty years earlier. His old Quinque links Aika’s weapon to both family
protection and the CCG’s violence against Ghouls.
Renji is Aika’s brother and an important trainer/protector. His relationship with Uta has
its own history; Itori’s stories about their younger years can be exaggerated and
corrected by the men.
Itori becomes Aika’s friend independently of Uta. Her bar is a social setting where Aika
learns about Ghoul culture and relationships.
Yuto’s place in Aika’s life grows through the Auction aftermath and later chapters.
Uta’s protectiveness develops until it is no longer only an extension of his attachment
to Aika.
Bjorn’s death in Chapter 74 is definitive and remains emotionally important. His old
registration/veterinary records later help the CCG investigator locate Aika and Uta in
## Chapter 83.

Yes — after actually checking the DGG file, I’d change that description. The current version is too
generic and slightly misleading about who Sato is.

The file establishes that Ms. Sato is an older household cook who has known
Aika since she was a child. Aika remembers her specifically as someone who
let her stay in the kitchen while she cooked, and Sato remembers Aika being
little. She’s cheerful, spirited, and maternal rather than simply “kind.” DGG
copy copy.pdf ( Dogs &amp; Girls &amp; Ghouls(Oh my!) Somanoko)

Her darker history is also specific: she was a former poisoner who poisoned
her first and second husbands. After that, she became part of the Kaneshiro
household and eventually served as its head cook. The file explicitly says she
no longer poisons people and is known for her excellent pies.

How Sato actually speaks

This  is  the  important  part:  Sato  is  soft-spoken,  polite,  maternal,  and
somewhat old-fashioned. The file explicitly characterizes her speech as “soft-
spoken, polite, maternal.” DGG copy copy.pdf ( Dogs &amp; Girls &amp;
Ghouls(Oh my!) Somanoko)


Her actual dialogue backs that up:

- “Hello Ms. Aika!”
- “It is so good to see you again!”
- “I remember when you were just this tall!”
- “I hope you don’t mind that I’ve made you a more traditional breakfast this
morning.”
- “Ms....May I ask something?”
- “Please...”
- “If you say that man with you is okay I shall take your word for it Ms.
## Aika...”
- “Of course...I apologize.”

She doesn’t speak like Kazuha—precise and professional—or like Merlin—
rough, folksy, contraction-heavy. Sato has a gentler, domestic register, with
polite phrasing, “shall,” “may I,” “I hope you don’t mind,” “of course,” etc. But
she’s not excessively formal. She can gossip, reminisce, get nervous, and talk
naturally about unpleasant things because of her past.

She also has a slightly old-fashioned, grandmotherly way of remembering
things. For example, when talking about Aika’s father and uncle, she casually
reminisces about their appetites and says:

“Scary days those were...and your father. He was impossible to cook for. He
liked nothing. Save for lemon cake...”

That combination is very Sato: warm domesticity + an unsettlingly casual
familiarity with the Kaneshiro family’s darker history.

Ms. Sato: Older household cook who has been with the Kaneshiro family since
Aika’s childhood. She was one of the few genuinely warm, maternal figures in
Aika’s upbringing and would let young Aika stay in the kitchen while she
cooked.  Cheerful,  spirited,  soft-spoken,  polite,  and  domestic;  she  has  a
grandmotherly way of reminiscing about Aika when she was little. She is also
a  former  poisoner  who  poisoned  her  first  and  second  husbands  before
becoming part of the Kaneshiro household. She no longer poisons people and
is now known for her cooking, particularly her excellent pies.

Speech: Soft-spoken, polite, maternal, and mildly old-fashioned. Uses gentle,
respectful phrasing such as “May I ask something?”, “I hope you don’t mind,”
“I shall take your word for it,” and “Of course...I apologize.” She speaks
warmly with Aika and can become nervous or fearful when discussing Ghouls,
but she isn’t stiff or excessively formal. Her manner is that of a kind older
cook/household aunt rather than a professional servant. She can reminisce,
gossip, and casually discuss the family’s disturbing history with an almost
domestic normalcy.

That’s much closer to the actual DGG Sato. The biggest correction I’d make

to the original is replacing “one of the few people genuinely kind to Aika” with
the more specific “one of the few warm, maternal figures who gave Aika a safe
place in the kitchen during childhood.” The chapters actually show that
relationship rather than merely labeling her kind. DGG copy copy.pdf ( Dogs
&amp; Girls &amp; Ghouls(Oh my!) Somanoko)

And one small but important distinction: Sato isn’t written as secretly sinister
because  she  was  a  poisoner.  Her  history  is  dark,  but  her  present
characterization is genuinely warm and domestic. That’s part of what makes
the “former poisoner → beloved household cook who makes pies” contrast
work.

So this is the corrected paragraph I’d use:


Merlin: Older, rugged former U.S. Navy man and ex-con; loyal Kaneshiro
household fixer and Aika’s longtime driver. He was one of the earliest
“misbegotten” members of the household. After being accused of killing a man in
a drunken fight, Aika’s father intervened, gave him his freedom and a second
chance, and Merlin became fiercely loyal to the family in return. He handles
driving, protection, and various unpleasant “fixes” for the household.

Personality: Rough but loyal, protective, folksy, gruff, practical, and frequently
joking. He has an older-brother/uncle-like familiarity with Aika and calls her
things like “Kiddo,” “Lil’ Miss,” and “Lil’ Lady.” Beneath the roughness, he is
deeply sentimental about the people who gave him a second chance. He believes
strongly in loyalty to those who stand by you.

Speech: Merlin speaks with a strong, casual, folksy accent. He uses contractions
constantly and deliberately roughens his grammar: “ain’t,” “ya,” “you’s,” “lil’,”
“’bout,” “’cept,” “fello’,” and similar forms. His sentences are loose and
conversational rather than polished. He jokes, teases, rambles, and sometimes
shifts from serious observations into casual humor without warning. His speech
should sound like an older working-class man who has spent decades around
criminals, sailors, and rough company—not like a formally educated
professional.

Voice: Warm underneath the gruffness, casually irreverent, occasionally crude,
and very familiar. Even when discussing violence or disturbing subjects, Merlin
tends to speak about them matter-of-factly rather than becoming solemn or
theatrical.

And one important correction if we’re keeping Kazuha and Merlin distinct:

Kazuha: formal, precise, restrained, professional even when irritated.
Merlin: rough, folksy, gruff, joking, contractions, strong casual accent.

The file actually gives us a great example of that contrast: Kazuha is standing
there with his hands behind his back, speaking formally while Merlin casually
interrupts him, calls him “Lil’ Kazu,” and tells Aika embarrassing stories about
him. DGG copy copy.pdf ( Dogs &amp; Girls &amp; Ghouls(Oh my!) Somanoko)

So if I write Merlin going forward, he should not sound like Kazuha with a few
“damn”s added. His sentence structure itself needs to be looser and more folksy.

I searched the DGG file for Hiroshi’s dialogue, his family relationship, the chapter
where Aika introduces him, and the scenes with Renji. There’s quite a bit of useful
characterization in those passages.
- Who Hiroshi is
Hiroshi is Aika’s biological uncle on her father’s side. He is her father’s brother.
The clearest confirmation comes in the family-reveal scene, when Renji asks whether
Hiroshi is actually related to Aika. Hiroshi answers:
“Yes. She is my family. By blood. Her father was my brother.”
So he isn’t an uncle by marriage or a family friend. He’s her paternal uncle, and his
existence as a Ghoul is one of the Kaneshiro family’s biggest buried secrets.
Aika introduces him as:

“The one and only Hiroshi Kaneshiro.”
She also jokes that they look practically like twins, flexing her arm beside his. Hiroshi
plays along, mentioning that Aika’s mother always said she looked more like him than
her father—and that her father wasn’t amused.
- His age
The file supports that Hiroshi is an adult man who has been a Ghoul for more than
twenty years. He tells Aika:
“I turned Ghoul more than 20 years ago. When you were still just a lil’ baby Glowbug.”
However, I couldn’t locate a reliable passage confirming his exact numerical age. The
material I found doesn’t establish whether he’s 42, 45, 48, or another age in his forties.
So, if Aika explicitly gives his age in another passage, I haven’t recovered that exact
line yet. I wouldn’t invent a number and treat it as established.
- How Hiroshi speaks
Hiroshi has a very recognizable voice. He’s casual, warm, teasing, and conversational,
but he’s not a caricature with an exaggerated accent.
A few things stand out:
- He uses affectionate nicknames. “Glowbug,” “Bug,” and “Kiddo” are familiar
names he’s used for Aika since she was little.
- He teases naturally. When Aika introduces Uta as her boyfriend, Hiroshi
immediately asks whether she’s old enough to have one.
- He has a playful sense of humor. When Aika jokes that they’re practically twins,
he joins in rather than dismissing her.
- He speaks plainly about serious subjects. When explaining his Ghoul
transformation and CCG history, he doesn’t become theatrical. He explains
things in a measured, matter-of-fact way.
- He occasionally corrects himself mid-sentence. For example, he says, “I quit—er,
fled my job,” which gives his speech a natural, unpolished quality.
- He can be openly affectionate and protective. When giving Aika his old Quinque,
he repeatedly explains that he wants her to have something that might keep her
safe.
He’s also comfortable making jokes around uncomfortable subjects. His humor doesn’t
disappear just because a conversation becomes serious.
- What Aika tells the others about him
Before the trip to his cabin, Aika admits to Uta, Renji, and Itori:

“...but there’s just one itty-bitty little thing about my uncle I didn’t mention? He...Well
he used to be in the CCG—Ages, and ages ago.”
Itori immediately reacts:
“Aika! That’s kind of a big deal!”
Aika explains that he left the CCG years ago, moved into the wilderness, and rarely
talks about his former job or Ghouls. She knows about his past partly because the
household staff used to share rumors about him.
She also tells them that he used to live with her family when she was very young. He
disappeared from Tokyo when she was little, and she didn’t see him again until she
was almost ten.
That makes an important distinction: Aika knows him as her uncle, someone who
taught her things and cared for her, not simply as a former CCG investigator.
- Renji’s dialogue and reactions
Renji actually gets some meaningful dialogue in the cabin scenes. He’s not just
standing silently in the background.
When he first meets Hiroshi, he is visibly tense and asks:
“Aika...this is your uncle? Is he related to you...?”
Hiroshi calmly confirms the blood relationship.
Later, once the group is eating, Renji makes a particularly perceptive observation
about Hiroshi’s living arrangements:
“It makes sense now why you chose to live here. Next to the forest.”
Hiroshi answers that people sometimes come into the forest to die, and that finding
food isn’t difficult. He explains that living this way is the only way he can stand
himself and retain some sense of humanity.
Renji recognizes the reference:
“Of course. Aokigahara—the sea of trees.”
Renji’s dialogue is restrained, but he is observant. He notices the implications of
Hiroshi’s lifestyle and doesn’t need to interrogate him constantly to understand what
he’s saying.
There’s also a later confrontation where Uta reacts to Hiroshi realizing that Aika has
brought three Ghouls to his cabin. Renji grabs Uta’s arm and tells him:

“Uta, wait—”
He tries to keep the situation calm rather than immediately escalating it.

One important detail for the new chapter: Hiroshi shouldn’t sound like Merlin. Merlin
has the much stronger folksy accent and rough working-class speech. Hiroshi’s
dialogue is more naturally casual and conversational, with teasing humor and
occasional self-corrections. He can be warm without sounding overly sentimental.

Found it! It’s in Chapter 51: “Weekend Away”, on Saturday morning, while Aika is
eating the fruit Uta prepared for her.
Uta tells her he’s looking forward to meeting her uncle. When she asks why, he
explains:
“I want to meet your uncle...Renji and Itori too.”
Then he says:
“I’m curious what he’s like....since he’s related to you.”
Aika pauses because she realizes Uta doesn’t have family members he can introduce
her to or compare childhood memories with. Then she answers:

“...yeah. He’s...he’s my fathers brother. You’ll like him I think. He’s like—A more
outgoing Renji? If Renji liked to talk to people and joke around more.”
Uta’s eyes widen a little.
“Really?”
And Aika adds:
“Yeah. Like I told you before; you’ll like him. Maybe he’ll get Renji talking and they’ll
be two of them, right?”
That’s the exact comparison you were looking for.
What Aika establishes about Hiroshi
- He’s her father’s brother—her biological paternal uncle.
- He’s like Renji in certain ways, but more outgoing.
- Unlike Renji, he’s talkative and enjoys joking around.
- Aika expects Uta to like him.
- She even imagines Hiroshi bringing Renji out of his shell, so the two of them
might become equally talkative.
What this means for writing Hiroshi
The distinction is important: Hiroshi isn’t simply a gruff, quiet older man who
occasionally makes jokes. Aika specifically describes him as a more sociable, talkative
version of Renji.
So his dialogue should have more conversational momentum. He initiates topics, asks
questions, jokes, teases, and keeps conversations moving. He can still become serious
and measured when discussing his Ghoul history, but his default social presence is
much more outgoing than Renji’s.
And Uta already has that expectation before he meets Hiroshi: he’s anticipating
someone who shares a little of Renji’s nature, but who actually enjoys talking.

Keiko’s story and how she connects to the others
- Interlude Chapter 1 — “A meeting in the rain”
This is Keiko’s actual introduction, told from Renji’s point of view.
Renji finds her standing on a bridge in the rain, apparently preparing to end her
life.
What draws her away from the railing is a box of abandoned kittens. She becomes
completely absorbed in trying to save them.
She  is  soaked,  freezing,  and  visibly  distressed,  but  she  keeps  holding  the
frightened kitten even while it bites her.
Renji eventually asks her name. She introduces herself as Keiko, shortened to Kei,
and says she lives a few blocks away.
He walks her home, helps her dry and clean the kittens, and tells her to keep
them.
The following day, he returns to check on them. He insists on accompanying her
to the pet store and eventually offers to share responsibility for the cats.
There is a particularly important detail here: Renji initially thinks of the kittens
as a reason to get Keiko talking. But he becomes involved himself. He returns
without really knowing why, accompanies her shopping, and pays for the supplies.
- Renji thinking about Aika and Uta in the interlude

This is the passage you specifically wanted me to look at.
When Keiko says she cannot keep the cats because her home isn't suitable, Renji
considers asking Uta. He immediately thinks of Aika, though:
“That woman that’s been hanging around him has a big dog.”
He then reflects on Aika's first meeting with the Ghoul group. He remembers that
she was friendly, a little nervous, and unusually eager to get to know them after
learning what they were.
Renji finds it surprising that Uta has made another friend, particularly a human
one. He compares it to the old woman who made masks, someone he thought would
be a once-in-a-lifetime exception.
Then comes the significant observation:
“Yet, when he watched how Aika had relaxed gradually even after only an hour or
two of knowing Uta’s friends Renji was sure she’d be sticking around.”
He remembers trying to warn her that Uta could be dangerous, but he already
suspects that warning won't change anything.
And then Renji thinks:
“Uta’s already rather attached to her, bringing her to a favorite perch. Not to
mention he’d even been asking Itori for some advice once in a while.”
That is a lovely bit of characterization because Renji is noticing Uta's behavior
from the outside. He sees that Uta is getting attached, that he is bringing Aika
into his familiar spaces, and that he's even asking Itori for advice.
Renji  recognizes  the  developing  attachment  before  either  Uta  or  Aika  has
necessarily put a name to it. And that thought occurs while he's considering
whether Uta might be a suitable person to help with Keiko's kittens.
- Chapter 22 — “Plans”
This chapter is mainly about Aika waiting at Uta's apartment while the Ghouls
organize the rescue of Kaneki.
It doesn't introduce Keiko, but it matters for the surrounding timeline: Aika is
already spending time at Uta's home, helping him, and becoming part of his
everyday life. The chapter also shows her growing familiarity with Ghoul life and
her willingness to trust Uta's circle.
- Chapter 23 — “SHOPPING!”
This chapter is significant for Aika and Uta's relationship rather than Keiko's.

Aika discovers that Uta's birthday was December 2 and realizes she missed it. She
immediately decides that they're going to have a party, messages Itori, and tells
her to inform Renji.
The  chapter  also  develops  Aika's  friendship  with  Itori.  Aika  admits  she's
intimidated by how beautiful, confident, and socially comfortable Itori is. She even
wonders whether she's feeling a little feminine competition because Itori has
known Uta for so much longer.
Itori is excited about Aika coming around, and Uta tells Aika that Itori asks about
her when she doesn't visit.
That  matters  later  because  Keiko  becomes  another  subject  of  conversation
between Aika and Renji, with Itori being the one who first starts poking around
about Renji's mysterious human companion.
- The later party and “Kitten” references
The later scenes make the nickname and the secret increasingly clear.
Itori notices that Renji smells like cats and suspects he's hiding a human from her
and Uta.
Aika hears about this and becomes curious.
She asks Renji about his “kittens,” but he doesn't want to discuss Keiko in front
of the other Ghouls.
Aika respects that and doesn't push him.
She later asks him about the cats and Keiko again, making it clear that her
interest isn't just Itori's gossip.
At one point, Aika teases Renji before he leaves on the rescue mission:
“You’ve got ‘kittens’ to watch. Don’t you?”
She deliberately means more than the actual cats. She's reminding him that
someone is waiting for him to come back.
And later, when Aika is speaking with Renji privately, she asks:
“So, Renji-kun. Who’s the ‘Kitten’ we hear almost nothing about?”
Renji tells her Keiko is just a friend. He also explains that Keiko found the strays
